reviewer: Independent AI relevance reviewer (not a human reviewer)
method: Blinded source-level abstract review of the 21 PMIDs in the independent worksheet. Grades: 2 directly answers the precise question, 1 limited contextual support, 0 no support. Only nonzero grades are listed; every unlisted source in the worksheet source_universe is grade 0. Existing 16 abstracts came only from data/indexes/rag_corpus_manifest.json; five added abstracts came from their PubMed records. No retrieval results or prior gold judgments were consulted.

evidence_anchors.34262598: Review identifies cannabis use among environmental factors repeatedly associated with schizophrenia.
evidence_anchors.37140715: Danish cohort reports elevated incident schizophrenia with registered cannabis use disorder, with adjusted HR 2.42 in males and 2.02 in females.

cases.reference_answer: Cannabis use is among the environmental exposures associated with schizophrenia. A Danish register study found higher subsequent schizophrenia incidence among people with cannabis use disorder, especially young males. These associations do not by themselves establish causation, and cannabis use disorder is a narrower exposure than any cannabis use.

evidence_anchors.34262598: Review describes complex genetic-environmental interplay, cannabis as an investigated schizophrenia exposure, and limited understanding of interactions.
evidence_anchors.37140715: CUD-schizophrenia association provides a cannabis-specific observational example without measuring genetic interaction.
evidence_anchors.25830477: Schizophrenia is associated with polygenic score and family socioeconomic/psychiatric background, without measuring cannabis.

cases.reference_answer: Psychosis vulnerability reflects genetic and environmental factors; cannabis use is among the exposures associated with schizophrenia. The available abstracts do not establish how cannabis specifically interacts with genetic liability or other environmental vulnerability, nor do they show that exposure is sufficient to cause psychosis.

evidence_anchors.38477889: Adjusted models found interactions between psychedelic use and genetic vulnerability to schizophrenia or bipolar I disorder for manic symptoms.

cases.reference_answer: Yes. In an adolescent twin study, the association of naturalistic psychedelic use with manic symptoms varied by genetic vulnerability to schizophrenia or bipolar I disorder. The observational findings warrant caution and do not establish that psychedelics cause mania.

evidence_anchors.23810828: Review explicitly states that genetic and environmental factors contribute to drug addiction.

cases.reference_answer: Yes. A review describes drug addiction as having both genetic and environmental contributions, with possible transgenerational epigenetic influences.

evidence_anchors.23810828: Review reports evidence of effects on descendants following parental preconception exposure to alcohol, nicotine, marijuana, opioids, or cocaine, even absent prenatal exposure.

cases.reference_answer: Possibly. A review describes evidence that parental exposure to abused drugs before conception may influence descendants' physiology or behavior, while mechanisms and human implications remain uncertain.

evidence_anchors.38446452: Twin cohort included adult clinical alcohol or drug misuse among psychiatric outcomes and found more ACEs associated with greater odds of any psychiatric disorder.

cases.reference_answer: ACEs were associated with a higher likelihood of adult clinically diagnosed psychiatric disorders in a twin cohort whose outcomes included alcohol or drug misuse. The abstract reports the association for a combined psychiatric outcome, so it does not quantify alcohol or drug misuse separately.

evidence_anchors.38446452: ACE association with combined adult psychiatric diagnoses persisted, though attenuated, in dizygotic and monozygotic twin comparisons; alcohol/drug misuse was one component.

cases.reference_answer: The association between ACEs and a combined adult psychiatric outcome, which included alcohol or drug misuse, remained after accounting for shared family factors in twin comparisons but weakened. The abstract does not report a separate family-adjusted estimate for substance outcomes.

evidence_anchors.24135711: Nonexperimental gene-environment studies can retain confounding when covariate-by-gene and covariate-by-environment terms are omitted.
evidence_anchors.38446452: Twin comparisons attenuated ACE associations, showing shared genetic/environmental family factors explain part of the crude association.
evidence_anchors.38718481: Childhood trauma and positive psychotic symptoms were analyzed cross-sectionally among people already diagnosed with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders.

cases.reference_answer: Observational ACE associations may reflect shared genes, family environment, measured or unmeasured confounding, and sometimes reverse or ambiguous temporal ordering. Twin comparisons reduce some shared-family confounding but do not prove causality; ordinary covariate adjustment can miss interaction-related confounding.

evidence_anchors.39648410: Nine-wave study associates repeated bullying victimization with higher depressive symptoms, with different cumulative patterns for girls and boys.
evidence_anchors.28562268: Fifth-grade peer victimization associated with seventh-grade depressive symptoms; repeated victimization was not separately evaluated in the abstract.
evidence_anchors.40625792: Cyberbullying victimization prospectively associated with depressive symptoms one year later; repeated exposure was not analyzed in the abstract.

cases.reference_answer: Yes. In a longitudinal study of South Korean adolescents from multicultural families, persistent bullying victimization was associated with higher depressive symptoms. The pattern differed by sex: an immediate, shorter pattern in girls and a cumulative pattern over three or more waves in boys.

evidence_anchors.39648410: Higher family support accompanied lower depressive symptoms among bullied girls; boys showed cumulative symptom increases regardless of support level.

cases.reference_answer: Family support was associated with lower depressive symptoms among bullied girls in the studied cohort, whereas bullied boys' cumulative increase appeared regardless of family support. The result is subgroup-specific and observational.

evidence_anchors.32997097: Primer says PRS alone cannot establish or definitively predict diagnoses of complex conditions because it captures only part of genetic and total risk.
evidence_anchors.25830477: Schizophrenia PRS explained 3.4% of liability in the reported sample; family factors also associated with risk.
evidence_anchors.32251439: Even a model with hundreds of predictors for adolescent mental health outcomes was considered unsuitable for clinical use; not a PRS study.

cases.reference_answer: No. A polygenic risk score estimates some genetic susceptibility but captures only part of the genetic contribution, while non-genetic factors also affect risk. It cannot determine an individual's future psychiatric diagnosis.

evidence_anchors.21382538: Prospective-study meta-analysis finds childhood ADHD associated with later nicotine, alcohol, marijuana, cocaine, and other abuse/dependence disorders.
evidence_anchors.29315559: ADHD cohort reports more frequent later substance use, but the abstract does not give disorder diagnoses.

cases.reference_answer: The expanded evidence does show an association: a meta-analysis of prospective studies found children with ADHD more likely to develop later substance abuse or dependence across several substances. A separate cohort supports higher later use, which is not itself a substance use disorder. Neither proves ADHD causes a disorder.

evidence_anchors.28562268: Earlier peer victimization was associated with later alcohol, marijuana, and tobacco use, not diagnosed SUD.
evidence_anchors.40625792: Cyberbullying victimization predicted later alcohol, nicotine, and cannabis experimentation, not SUD.

cases.reference_answer: These abstracts link peer or cyberbullying victimization with later substance use or experimentation. They do not measure or establish a later substance use disorder, so the specific victimization-to-SUD association remains unsupported by this source set.

evidence_anchors.21382538: Longitudinal meta-analysis reports elevated later abuse/dependence disorders for nicotine, alcohol, marijuana, cocaine, and other substances among children with ADHD.
evidence_anchors.29315559: Childhood ADHD cohort shows elevated later use rather than abuse/dependence diagnosis.

cases.reference_answer: Yes. A meta-analysis of prospective studies associated childhood ADHD with higher later rates of substance abuse or dependence for several substances. Comorbid disruptive behavior disorders complicate attributing the association specifically to ADHD; causation is not established.

evidence_anchors.29315559: Young-adult weekly marijuana use was 32.8% in ADHD versus 21.3% in comparison participants; daily smoking was 35.9% versus 17.5%.

cases.reference_answer: Yes. By young adulthood, weekly marijuana use was 32.8% versus 21.3%, and daily cigarette smoking was 35.9% versus 17.5%, for the childhood-ADHD and comparison groups, respectively. These are use outcomes, not SUD diagnoses.

evidence_anchors.21382538: The prospective meta-analysis says children with ADHD were more likely ever to use nicotine and other substances, but not alcohol.

cases.reference_answer: No. The prospective meta-analysis did not find significantly greater ever-use of alcohol among children with ADHD, despite finding elevated later alcohol abuse/dependence.

evidence_anchors.28562268: Fifth-grade peer victimization linked indirectly to tenth-grade alcohol, marijuana, and tobacco use through seventh-grade depressive symptoms.
evidence_anchors.40625792: Cyberbullying victimization linked to one-year-later experimentation in the same substance classes; distinct exposure and outcome timing.

cases.reference_answer: Yes. In a longitudinal cohort, more frequent fifth-grade peer victimization was associated with greater tenth-grade alcohol, marijuana, and tobacco use, with seventh-grade depressive symptoms a modeled mediator. The study is observational and reports use, not SUD.

evidence_anchors.40625792: Year-2 cyberbullying victimization predicted greater year-3 alcohol, nicotine, and cannabis experimentation after adjustment for baseline outcomes and demographics.
evidence_anchors.28562268: Traditional peer victimization linked with later use, not specifically cyberbullying or experimentation.

cases.reference_answer: Yes. In a prospective cohort of early adolescents, cyberbullying victimization was associated with higher odds one year later of alcohol, nicotine, and cannabis experimentation. This does not establish causality or a substance use disorder.

evidence_anchors.33224066: PubMed abstract reports a positive within-person association from bullying at age 12 to smoking/drinking at age 13, with no reverse effect; abstract does not explicitly define bullying as perpetration.

cases.reference_answer: The study reports that bullying at age 12 predicted smoking or drinking at age 13. Its PubMed abstract does not explicitly specify whether the bullying measure represents perpetration rather than victimization, so the perpetration-specific reading requires verification against the full text.

evidence_anchors.28562268: Peer-victimization cohort measured subsequent alcohol, marijuana, and tobacco use, not SUD, and used observational structural-equation modeling.
evidence_anchors.40625792: Cybervictimization cohort measured experimentation one year later, not SUD, and used observational regression.
evidence_anchors.33224066: Bullying study measured smoking/drinking, not SUD; abstract does not establish that exposure is victimization.

cases.reference_answer: No. The relevant victimization studies report later use or experimentation, not diagnosed substance use disorder. Their observational designs cannot establish that victimization causes a later SUD. The additional bullying study also measured smoking and drinking and its abstract does not clearly identify victimization as the exposure.

uncertainties: PMID 33224066: the PubMed abstract calls the exposure 'bullying' without explicitly stating perpetration or victimization; the perpetration-specific grade 2 is provisional pending full-text measurement verification in adjudication.

PMID 38446452: the abstract includes alcohol/drug misuse in a combined psychiatric outcome but gives no substance-specific effect estimate; grades for ACE-01 and ACE-02 reflect this direct inclusion with a bounded answer.
The negative SUD questions distinguish absence of an endpoint in these sources from evidence of no true association.
